analysis.one_liner: Caps donations to super PACs at the same limit as regular PACs, ending unlimited megadonor giving.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2025 with 33 Democratic cosponsors, the bill to cap super PAC donations has sat in the House Administration Committee ever since, with no hearing, no vote, and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The Abolish Super PACs Act would apply normal PAC contribution limits — currently $5,000 per donor per year — to super PACs, the committees that can now accept unlimited checks and spend it all on elections. The bill's own findings note that independent spending topped $4.48 billion in 2024, spread across 2,459 super PACs, and that the top 1% of individual super PAC donors supplied nearly 97% of individual super PAC contributions that year. It was referred to the House Administration Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, and candidates who lack megadonor backing. Capping super PAC contributions at ordinary PAC levels would shrink the role of a tiny class of nine-figure donors, reduce the risk that super PACs are used as a channel for corrupt deals between donors and candidates, cut off a route for foreign money funneled in through third parties, and — as the bill's findings argue — restore public confidence that elections are not bought [S2]. Candidates who spend time with small donors instead of courting billionaires would face a more even field [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Federal Election Campaign Act so that super PACs (defined as committees spending $5,000 or more on independent expenditures) are subject to the same contribution limit as any other political committee — effectively ending their ability to accept unlimited money from a single donor, which is why it is titled the Abolish Super PACs Act.

Would reduce the dominance of a tiny donor class: the bill's findings state the top 1% of individual super PAC contributors gave 76.76% of all individual super PAC contributions in 2012, rising to 96.94% in 2024, with recent elections shaped by individuals giving more than $100 million.

Would curb corruption risk and its appearance — the findings argue super PACs can serve as conduits for corrupt agreements between donors and candidates, citing prosecutions where bribes were funneled through super PACs — and would make it harder for foreign entities to funnel money into elections through third-party contributors.

analysis.who_pays: Super PACs and the wealthy individuals who fund them. The bill's findings record $4.48 billion in independent expenditures in 2024 across 2,459 registered super PACs, nearly all of it from the top 1% of donors [S2]. Political advertising agencies, consultants, and media outlets that earn fees on that spending would also see the pool of money shrink [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Super PACs and their wealthy donors

drawbacks.text: The cap would almost certainly face a First Amendment court challenge. The bill's own findings concede that the D.C. Circuit's SpeechNow.org v. FEC decision voided existing contribution limits to super PACs in 2010; unless the Supreme Court reverses that reasoning, a statutory cap risks being struck down, leaving donors' money intact and the law nullified.

Because the bill caps contributions but does not ban spending outright, big money could migrate to channels the bill does not touch — such as nonprofit groups that do not have to disclose donors — potentially making campaign money less transparent, not more.

The bill does not alter the underlying Citizens United framework that permits unlimited independent spending; reformers who favor a constitutional amendment to reverse that precedent may view a statutory cap as a partial and litigable fix.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stakes are large: an election money system in which 2,459 super PACs spent $4.48 billion in 2024, with nearly 97% of individual super PAC money from the top 1% of donors, would be rebalanced toward ordinary contributors and candidates without billionaire backing [S2]. The main weaknesses are that the cap sits in tension with existing court precedent and that money can move to undisclosed channels — an honest supporter would say this bill is a down payment on reform that courts or future Congresses would have to finish. Its biggest practical cost so far is political: it has received no committee action and no Republican support, so none of these effects are close to taking place.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Administration Committee on the day it was introduced and has sat there since, with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action; Congress is still in session, so it technically remains alive.

narrative.text: Representative Summer Lee of Pennsylvania introduced the Abolish Super PACs Act on March 26, 2025, with six original cosponsors: Representatives Khanna, McGovern, Jayapal, Tlaib, Deluzio, and Ramirez.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on House Administration, the panel that handles election and campaign finance legislation.
Thirty-three House Democrats signed on as cosponsors — no Republicans did — and since the March 2025 referral the bill has seen no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Super PACs and their biggest donors are better off so far: the unlimited-contribution system the bill targets — $4.48 billion spent in 2024, nearly all from the top 1% of individual donors — continues untouched while the bill sits in committee [S2].

for.name: Summer Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Abolish Super PACs Act and shepherded it to committee referral.

for.name: Ro Khanna, Jim McGovern, Pramila Jayapal, Rashida Tlaib, Chris Deluzio, and Delia Ramirez
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: 27 additional House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Brought the total to 33 cosponsors, all Democrats; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Bryan Steil
against.role: Chair, House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Committee received the bill on referral in March 2025 and has taken no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Controls the House and its committee agenda
against.what_they_did: No Republican member cosponsored the bill and the House has not considered it; the majority sets which bills get committee time and floor votes.

against.name: Super PAC networks and their large donors
against.what_they_did: Benefit from the unlimited-contribution system the bill would cap; outside groups aligned with big-money fundraising have long opposed contribution limits of this kind.

sides.party_line_note: All 33 cosponsors are Democrats and the bill's introduction was entirely Democratic; no Republican has signed on and the Republican-run committee has taken no action on it.

industries.note: The bill caps their contributions at the ordinary PAC limit, ending the unlimited-dollar model that produced $4.48 billion in 2024 spending across 2,459 registered super PACs. Their core revenue channel would be shut off in the first calendar year after enactment.

The top 1% of individual super PAC contributors supplied 96.94% of individual super PAC contributions in 2024, and some individuals have given more than $100 million. A $5,000-per-donor cap would end their outsize leverage over elections.
Consultants, ad buyers, and media outlets collect fees on super PAC spending; shrinking the money pool shrinks their business, while the public interest runs the other way.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is very likely to die quietly in committee. Campaign finance bills from House Democrats have not received hearings or votes under the Republican majority, the committee chair has taken no action in the months since referral, and the bill has no Republican cosponsors — the same pattern that befell prior versions of this proposal in earlier Congresses.
